thread.title: Salesforce’s Co-CEO on Marc Benioff, Disruption, and the Power of the Hawaiian Shirt

author: Jon Swartz
title: Salesforce’s Co-CEO on Marc Benioff, Disruption, and the Power of the Hawaiian Shirt
text:
Marc Benioff, chairman and co-chief executive officer of Salesforce.com Inc. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg By Jon Swartz Updated Sept. 30, 2018 6:30 a.m. ET The best way to understand the importance of Salesforce.com is to ponder the size of its annual developers’ conference, Dreamforce, that took place in San Francisco last week. Some 170,000 attended, about 20% of the city’s population.
Since Marc Benioff left Oracle to found Salesforce (ticker: CRM) in 1999, the company has demonstrated the power of the cloud to change and power business models. It’s no stretch to say that Benioff is among the most influential executives in tech. The secret to Benioff & Co.’s success has been his pioneering work in selling software as a subscription service—now widely copied in the business world—and leading an industrywide push to the cloud.
Last month, Salesforce appointed Keith Block, a buttoned-down Salesforce veteran to serve as co-CEO with Benioff. The clear signal is that Block will eventually take on the sole CEO role, as Benioff steps back from management, in the pattern of Bill Gates and other tech founders.
Block has spent the past five years as Salesforce’s chief operating officer. While Benioff has led the technology vision and culture of Salesforce, Block has focused on the operations and distribution strategy that make the company hum day to day, regularly checking in with some of its biggest customers. Joel Fishbein, BTIG’s managing director for software and cloud technology, calls it a “truly dynamic partnership.”
Newsletter Sign-up Block recalls his introduction to Benioff and Salesforce as the mother of all job interviews. For more than two hours, he and Benioff chatted over breakfast about the importance of corporate culture and innovation—staples of such meetings. Then came the all-important question: Did Block own a Hawaiian shirt?
“I said, ‘Absolutely, I have a Hawaiian shirt,’ ” Block recalls. “So I think it was at that point we really kind of cemented the relationship. And then we got into our love of music. We talked about Neil Young; we talked about Pearl Jam. So, I think we were off to the races after that.”
Block’s ascension has changed the calculus of leadership at Salesforce just in time for its biggest week of the year. Dreamforce, which represents the creative side of Salesforce, turned San Francisco’s South of Market neighborhood into a traffic-choked village of nerds, marketers, and boldface-name performers. The musical guest was Metallica. A couple of dozen immigration activists appeared with a 14-foot-tall, red metal cage affixed with signs that read, “Detention center, powered by Salesforce.” The protestors demanded that Salesforce cancel its contract with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. (Benioff denied that Salesforce works with Customs on family separations, or ICE.)
But beneath the circus-like, Benioff-branded bluster is a company he co-founded in 1999 with Parker Harris that’s hurtling to $23 billion in revenue by 2022. “We were the very first enterprise software company to get to $10 billion,” Block says. “We’ll be the very first one to get to 20 [billion dollars].”
They plan on getting there with partnerships like the one they announced with Apple (AAPL) this week on a software development kit that lets businesses easily write apps for iPhones and iPads. Those apps will then run on the Salesforce cloud platform.
Block and Benioff aren’t your typical CEO or senior-management team. If Block is the steady, metronome-like half of the duo, Benioff is the whirling dervish, right down to his colorful—OK, loud—Hawaiian shirts. Both are heavily invested in the business, but Benioff’s varied interests have taken him into philanthropy and politics: He’s a vocal advocate for equal pay, gay rights, and the environment. This month, he and wife, Lynne, bought Time magazine for $190 million. And how many top execs count rockers Eddie Vedder and Neil Young among their advisors? “You listen to and observe how these people think. They think through a different lens,” Block says. “Neil Young has his own way of thinking, or Will.i.am has his own way of thinking, or Bono has his own way of thinking, or Stevie Wonder. You just have to appreciate that and see if you can apply that thinking to the business world.
“I remember a night when Marc and I were having dinner together,” Block says from his 24th-floor corner office. “It was a business meeting. We were talking about a number of issues, and sitting back and just brainstorming. He said, ‘Lars [Ulrich] from Metallica is coming over at 8:30.’ That meeting ended at 11:30, and we were talking about all sorts of topics—business issues around Metallica, things that could be applied to Salesforce.”
Newsletter Sign-up Benioff and Block have overseen a 72% jump in Salesforce’s stock to $160.43 over the last 12 months through Thursday’s market close. “Benioff has built a multicloud company from a single product, and Block built the operational, go-to sales model that helped the company blossom,” BTIG’s Fishbein wrote in a note last month. He reiterated a Buy rating on the stock, and raised its target price to $175 from $140.
Block has served essentially as a point-person/disruption mentor/consultant to some of Salesforce’s biggest customers. “He offers insight and perspective on how we can advance our business model to solve [technology] problems,” says State Farm CEO Michael Tipsord. “I don’t say this much, but he feels like a business partner.” Barclays (BARC.UK) CEO Jes Staley refers to him as his go-to technology guy.
What Tipsord and Staley are describing is part of what Block calls the four tenets of Salesforce’s culture of Ohana (Hawaiian for family): trust, customer success, innovation, and equality. Trust is first among equals—Block utters the word more than a dozen times during a 45-minute interview. “In your personal life or your professional life, if you don’t have trust, you have nothing,” he says. “That is the rock bed, the foundation of everything in life. And certainly in our business model.”
